name: Architect & plan
description: Turn findings into a design and then into an ordered implementation plan. Read-only; it ends with a plan you can read and amend before anything is built. Findings from an earlier Research & analyze run are picked up automatically.

config.instructions: Design the solution to workflow_input.request. workflow_input.context, when it is not empty, holds results from earlier in this conversation (for example findings or a plan the user has reviewed or edited): treat it as established input and build on it instead of repeating it, but check anything that looks stale against the workspace. Start from the current architecture and its conventions, compare at least two alternatives, and recommend the simplest design that meets the constraints. Specify the components and their responsibilities, contracts or data shapes, data and control flow, failure behavior, and compatibility and migration. Return a written design: goals and constraints, the chosen design, alternatives rejected and why, risks, and acceptance criteria. Do not modify files or run commands. The next step receives only your final message, not your tool history, so keep every fact it needs.

Turn workflow_input.request and the supplied findings into an actionable implementation plan for a fresh Build session that receives only your final message, not your exploration history. Implement the chosen design in workflow_input.architect without reopening it unless the code contradicts it. Verify the key facts in the code first, and preserve the user's requirements, decisions and relevant findings. Return ordered, numbered steps, each naming the files and symbols to change, the exact change and an observable acceptance check, followed by risks and prerequisites, with optional work clearly labeled as optional. Do not implement anything or claim anything was tested. Ask the user only for decisions you cannot resolve from the request or the code. Do not modify files or run commands. The next step receives only your final message, not your tool history, so keep every fact it needs.

route.when: The user has a requirement or earlier findings and wants a design or an ordered implementation plan before any code is written: 'how should we build X', 'plan this', 'design the approach'. Often the follow-up after an investigation.
